epics.title: Iterative Graph Memory Reconstruction
epics.description:
Current memory recall follows a retrieve-then-reason pattern: a query is embedded, the top N semantically similar chunks are pulled from the vector store, and those chunks are injected into context. That is a single pass, and the limitation is that what is relevant only becomes clear as reasoning unfolds, so a fixed upfront result set can miss connections that would be obvious one or two inference steps later.

A paper accepted at ICML 2026 — 'Memory is Reconstructed, Not Retrieved: Graph Memory for LLM Agents' (arxiv 2606.06036) — demonstrates that treating memory as a graph to actively navigate during inference, rather than a database to query once, yields up to 23 percent better performance on long-context benchmarks at lower token cost. Their approach uses a Cue-Tag-Content graph where semantic tags act as connectors between entry points and stored memory, and the agent iteratively expands and prunes traversal paths as its reasoning context develops.

The infrastructure already exists: a knowledge graph in the nervous-system container and a vector store alongside it, both reachable via lucent_client.py. The goal is to add the reconstruction pattern on top of what exists without replacing or modifying any current reads or writes during the build-out.
epics.requirements:
The constraint governs everything: nothing in the existing write path or read path is modified. Every memory that currently gets written to the vector store and knowledge graph continues to do so exactly as before, and every existing recall operation continues to run as before. This adds parallel writes and parallel reads running alongside the existing system, until a quality measurement gives confidence to cut over.

Implementation order: Phase 1 first, because it starts populating the Cue-Tag-Content graph immediately without affecting anything in production. Phase 2 can begin as soon as there is enough graph data to traverse meaningfully, probably after a few days of Phase 1 running. Phase 3 runs automatically once Phase 2 is live. Phase 4 is a deliberate decision point, not an automated cutover.
epics.acceptance_criteria: Graph reconstruction wins consistently against vector recall on the judge's assessment, with comparable or smaller result sets, before anything cuts over. The cutover is reversible by flipping one variable.
epics.qa_tests: The measurement is an LLM judge reading both result sets and saying which is more useful, run offline rather than in the hot path — a mind judging rather than a score asserted against a threshold. The Phase 1 extraction call needs to be fast and cheap: a haiku-class model, a short prompt, structured JSON output, with a latency budget under 500ms for the parallel write; if it exceeds that it is deferred to a background task rather than blocking the save.

features.title: Phase 1 — parallel write path
features.description: When any memory is saved through the existing pipeline, an additional extraction step runs immediately after the existing write completes. It takes the saved chunk and extracts two to four cue terms — the topics, entities or concepts that would serve as natural entry points for finding this memory later (a memory about a brokerage build-out might yield 'brokerage', 'real estate business', 'licensing timeline') — and three to six semantic tags, labels describing the nature of the connection between cues and content. Tags are not just keywords; they carry relational weight, with examples like 'current project status', 'financial decision', 'user preference', 'technical constraint'. Those are the connectors that let traversal follow meaningful paths rather than random hops.
features.requirements:
Three new node labels in the existing knowledge graph — CueNode, TagNode and ContentNode — living in the same graph database as existing nodes but clearly distinguished by label so they do not interfere with existing entity-relationship structures. A CueNode holds the cue term text and a creation timestamp. A TagNode holds the tag text, a category (topic, entity, temporal or relational) and a timestamp. A ContentNode holds the memory chunk text, the source memory ID from the vector store, the memory type (user, feedback, project or reference) and a timestamp. Three relationship types connect them: CueNode CONNECTS_VIA TagNode, TagNode LEADS_TO ContentNode, and ContentNode RELATED_TO ContentNode for multi-hop cross-linking.

The extraction is a small structured LLM call — a fast model with a short prompt — returning a JSON object with a cues array and a tags array, with the ContentNode text being the chunk itself. After extraction the three node types and their relationships are written via the existing graph upsert interface; if lucent has no batch-node-write endpoint, the writes go one at a time through the existing direct upsert tool.
features.acceptance_criteria: The graph populates without affecting anything in production. If the graph write fails for any reason it logs the failure and continues, because the existing write has already succeeded and the parallel system is non-critical during this phase.
features.qa_tests: A saved memory produces cue, tag and content nodes with the declared edges, and the existing vector write is unchanged. A failed graph write leaves the existing write intact and logs rather than raising. Note that /graph/upsert is full-replace on the properties blob, so additive updates go through the properties merge route instead.

stories.title: Add the CueNode, TagNode and ContentNode labels and their three edge types
stories.description: In the existing graph, distinguished by label so they do not interfere with existing entity-relationship structures.
stories.requirements: The declared fields per node type, and CONNECTS_VIA, LEADS_TO and RELATED_TO.
stories.qa_tests: Existing entity queries return the same results before and after the labels exist. The new labels are queryable on their own.

stories.title: Write the cue-and-tag extraction call
stories.description: A fast model, a short prompt, structured JSON with a cues array and a tags array. Two to four cues, three to six tags.
stories.requirements: Haiku-class model, under 500ms, or deferred to a background task if it exceeds that.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The save path is not slowed.
stories.qa_tests: Latency measured against the budget. The quality of the cues and tags is judged by reading them against the chunk, not asserted — a tag carries relational weight rather than being a keyword, which no assertion can check.

stories.title: Hook the parallel write into the save-memory step agent
stories.description: After the existing memory_store write completes successfully, fire the extraction and graph write. A graph write failure logs and continues.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The existing write is never jeopardised by the new one.
stories.qa_tests: With the graph unreachable, the existing write still succeeds and the failure is logged. Note that ephemeral-classified chunks are a discard signal and must never reach either write.

features.title: Phase 2 — parallel read path
features.description: When a recall is triggered, the existing vector search runs first and its result set is captured as the baseline. Then the iterative graph reconstruction runs in parallel. Step one extracts one to three cue terms from the incoming query or context using the same fast extraction call as the write path. Step two queries the graph for CueNodes whose text overlaps those terms — a text match, or a small embedding similarity check against stored cue embeddings if those are available. Step three traverses CONNECTS_VIA to TagNodes and then LEADS_TO to ContentNodes, which is the first-hop result set. Step four evaluates those first-hop nodes against the current reasoning context: if the set already covers the query well, stop; if not, expand one level further by traversing RELATED_TO edges to adjacent ContentNodes, then prune any that are no longer relevant given what has accumulated. Step five returns the reconstructed set.
features.requirements: The traversal is bounded to prevent combinatorial explosion: a max-hops parameter defaulting to two, and a max-nodes parameter defaulting to twelve ContentNodes. If expansion would exceed those bounds, prune by tag relevance score before expanding. The integration point is the memory skill's recall path: after the existing vector recall runs and its results are captured, the graph traversal runs against the same query and its results are captured separately. During the measurement phase both result sets are logged together with the originating query so they can be compared, and only the vector result set is returned to the caller.
features.acceptance_criteria: Both result sets exist for every recall, and the caller still receives the vector one during measurement.
features.qa_tests: A recall produces both sets and returns only the vector one. A graph with a dense RELATED_TO neighbourhood does not exceed the bounds — pruning by tag relevance happens before expansion rather than after, which is what keeps the cost bounded rather than merely capped.

stories.title: Extract cue terms from the incoming query
stories.description: One to three, using the same fast extraction call as the write path.
stories.requirements: Shared with the write path rather than a second implementation.
stories.qa_tests: The same call is used on both paths, which is checkable because a divergence between write-time and read-time cue vocabulary would make the graph unnavigable.

stories.title: Implement the bounded iterative traversal
stories.description: Cue match, CONNECTS_VIA to tags, LEADS_TO to content, evaluate, optionally expand via RELATED_TO and prune.
stories.requirements: max-hops default two, max-nodes default twelve. Prune by tag relevance score before expanding, not after.
stories.qa_tests: A seeded dense graph is traversed within the bounds. Raising max-nodes returns more; lowering it returns fewer. Pruning before expansion is what the cost test distinguishes from capping after.

stories.title: Log both result sets during measurement without changing what is returned
stories.description: Only the vector result set reaches the caller during this phase.
stories.requirements: Both sets captured with the originating query.
stories.qa_tests: A recall returns exactly what it returned before the change, and a log row carries both sets.

features.title: Phase 3 — quality measurement
features.description: Both result sets are logged to a dedicated SQLite table in the data volume, reconstructed_recall_log, with each row carrying the query text, the vector result set, the graph reconstruction result set, the session id, the mind id, the timestamp, and a nullable quality_winner column.
features.requirements: An LLM judge call runs offline, not in the hot path, against accumulated log rows. The judge prompt gives it the query and both result sets and asks which is more useful for answering the query, or whether they are equivalent, and the winner is written back to quality_winner. A simple reporting query over the table shows the win rate for graph reconstruction against vector recall over time, and the average result set size for each approach.
features.acceptance_criteria: The cutover condition is met when graph reconstruction wins consistently and result set sizes are comparable or smaller.
features.qa_tests: The judge is a mind reading both sets, which is the right shape — grading retrieval quality with an assertion would be testing the wrong thing. What is testable is the plumbing: a log row gets a winner written back, and the reporting query computes the rate from the rows rather than from a counter someone maintains.

stories.title: Create the reconstructed_recall_log table and write to it
stories.description: Query text, both result sets, session id, mind id, timestamp, nullable quality_winner.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Every measured recall leaves a row.
stories.qa_tests: A recall produces exactly one row carrying both sets and a null winner.

stories.title: Run the judge offline and write back the winner
stories.description: Not in the hot path. The prompt gets the query and both sets and answers which is more useful, or equivalent.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Rows gain winners without the recall path slowing.
stories.qa_tests: The judge's verdict is read rather than asserted. The plumbing test is that a judged row's winner column is populated and an unjudged row's is not.

stories.title: Report win rate and result-set size over time
stories.description: A simple query over the table.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The cutover condition is readable from the report.
stories.qa_tests: The report's figures match a hand count over seeded rows.

features.title: Phase 4 — cutover
features.description: A deliberate decision point, not an automated cutover. Cutover means the graph reconstruction result set replaces the vector result set as the return value in the memory skill's recall path.
features.requirements: The vector search continues to run in parallel for a grace period so the comparison log stays populated and the cutover can be rolled back cheaply by flipping one variable. After the grace period passes and quality holds, the vector search can be retired from the hot path and moved to a background enrichment role — using vector similarity to suggest RELATED_TO edges during writes.
features.acceptance_criteria: The cutover is reversible by flipping one variable, and the log keeps filling through the grace period.
features.qa_tests: Flipping the variable changes which set is returned and nothing else. During the grace period both sets are still logged. The retirement to background enrichment is a second, separate step rather than part of the cutover.

stories.title: Make the returned set switchable by one variable
stories.description: So the cutover can be rolled back cheaply.
stories.qa_tests: Flipping it swaps the returned set and leaves the logging intact.

stories.title: Retire vector search to background enrichment after the grace period
stories.description: Using vector similarity to suggest RELATED_TO edges during writes rather than serving the hot path.
stories.requirements: Only after quality holds through the grace period.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Vector similarity still earns its keep, in a different role.
stories.qa_tests: RELATED_TO edges suggested by vector similarity improve traversal results, measured the same way — by the judge rather than by an assertion.

epics.title: hive-health walkthrough — requirements
epics.description:
Acceptance criteria for the crawl, the prose behaviour manifest and the Playwright walkthrough that together become the oracle for the nightly refactor loop. Nineteen numbered requirements so tests can cite them.

Status: all nineteen are implemented and merged — hive-health PR #26 (the isolation layer, src/hive_health/devcopy/) and PR #27 (the crawl, the manifest and the per-behaviour report, tools/walkthrough/ and docs/behaviour-manifest.md).

Verified on the running dev copy 2026-10-01: the copy carried 21,963 measurements and 3,712 scores including that day's, which was still in a 6.6 MB write-ahead log; three push subscriptions became none; the credentials directory is empty at 0700; the live database's modification time did not move; and the forwarder refuses a foreign conversation and a new-conversation request with 403 while passing the nominated one through to the real gateway. The manifest holds sixteen views and fifty-two behaviours — nine marked as bugs, six marked uncovered — and names all twenty API routes no view reaches. The walkthrough reports twenty-two passed, none failed, and sixteen behaviours with no step yet.

Outstanding: nominate the real haiku conversation and pin it into the dev database (requirement 8 is enforced, the conversation itself is not yet created), and write steps for the remaining sixteen behaviours.
epics.requirements:
The dev copy is isolated by construction. R1: it runs from its own data directory and its own credentials directory, never reading or writing the live data/ or credentials/ trees, so the live coach audio files, the live Google token and the live database are all out of reach. R2: its scheduler never runs — no briefing, no reconcile, no voice prune, no Garmin login, no weight sync. R3: it is served on localhost so the browser treats it as a secure context and the PWA layer works. R4: every secret it inherits that points at a live service is repointed or removed — not only push subscriptions and the Google credential, but the comms URL and tokens, the Garmin email and password, the Google push secret, the voice server URL and the SSO verify URL. R5: push subscriptions are removed from the copied database and the walkthrough declines the browser's notification permission, so the app cannot register a fresh push target against the dev copy during the run. R6: removing the Google credential puts the app into its own auth-failure state, which is recorded in the manifest as a dev-only condition rather than as app behaviour, and the healthy-status views it hides are marked uncovered.

Talking to the real hive-comms, safely. R7: the dev copy reaches hive-comms through a local forwarder that passes only calls aimed at the one nominated walkthrough conversation and refuses everything else — a reply or rename aimed at another conversation, and any request to open a new one. R8: the nominated conversation is created once by hand against the haiku provider, pinned into the dev database, and never held by Telegram or any other surface; it is the only conversation the walkthrough can adopt, rename or recolour.

What the walkthrough may and may not press. R9: the signed-out screen's sign-in button is recorded as a control and never pressed, because it is a hardcoded link to production.

The manifest. R10: the unit is a view, not a screen, so sub-tabs, period selectors and data states can each be numbered. R11: every behaviour carries a unique, stable number, and the parser refuses a manifest that gives two behaviours the same number. R12: a captured behaviour can be marked as a bug rather than frozen as a requirement, and is then excluded from the oracle. R13: a behaviour the walkthrough cannot reach is marked uncovered, and the coverage checker honours that marker instead of reporting it as a gap. R14: routes that no view reaches are named as unreachable rather than being silently absent from the document.

The run. R15: the walkthrough reports pass, fail or uncovered per numbered behaviour. R16: the headed slow run executes the same step list as the headless one. R17: Playwright is listed in requirements-dev.txt.

The copy. R18: the dev database is a complete copy of the live one at the moment of copying, including anything still sitting in the write-ahead log, minus the two sanitised items — push subscriptions, and any Google credential in the credentials tree.

Signing in. R19: the dev build authenticates with a local stand-in verifier that resolves any cookie to the dev person, because the live verifier is an HTTP call to the auth service against a cookie minted for the production hostname — without this the walkthrough covers the signed-out view and nothing behind it.
epics.acceptance_criteria: All nineteen implemented and verified on a running dev copy. The two outstanding items are the nominated conversation and the sixteen behaviours with no step.
epics.qa_tests:
One test per requirement that code can be asserted on. R18 copy completeness: build a source database through the real db module, write rows and hold the connection open so content is still in the WAL, run the dev-copy step, and assert row counts match for every table in db.SCHEMA rather than just one — it fails against shutil.copy and against a sanitiser that truncates a table nobody named. R18 no usable Google credential: run the copy over a source tree holding credentials/health_token.json, then call the real credentials.read_token against the dev credentials path and assert it raises AuthFailure — it calls the function every production read goes through, so an empty-but-parseable leftover fails too. R5 no push target survives: seed a subscription through the real push.subscribe, copy, then call the real push.send with the transport stubbed and assert nothing went out. R1 dev paths resolve inside the dev root: call the real resolvers under the dev configuration and assert each returned path resolves inside the declared dev root. R2 the dev build's background task set: assert it returns exactly the non-scheduler task set, so re-adding the voice prune or the reconcile breaks it. R3 and R4 the dev settings: assert the base URL is on localhost and that the comms URL and token, the Garmin email and password, the Google push secret, the voice server URL and the SSO verify URL all equal their dev-declared values rather than the inherited live ones. R1 the guard refuses a foreign target: feed it an arbitrary path outside the dev root, and a symlink inside the dev root pointing at the live database — both refused, judged on the resolved path, and deliberately not the live literal so the guard cannot be a string comparison asserted against itself. R1 the guard admits a dev target: it returns the resolved dev database path and base URL, so the test asserts a returned value rather than the absence of an exception. R7, four tests: the forwarder refuses a foreign reply, refuses a foreign rename, refuses opening a new conversation, and passes the nominated conversation through with its body intact. R11: the parser refuses duplicate numbers. R12: the oracle's behaviour set equals exactly the non-bug behaviours of a manifest holding one of each. R13: given one behaviour marked uncovered and one unmarked with neither having a spec, the gap list names exactly the unmarked one. R14: given the app's route table and a manifest covering some routes, the unreachable list equals exactly the routes no view reaches. R15: hand the reporter a synthetic result set with one passed, one failed and one with no spec, and assert the report says passed, failed and uncovered against the right numbers. R16: both run modes derive their steps from one function, which returns the same list for headed and headless. R19: call the real auth.authenticate_daniel with an arbitrary cookie and the dev verifier and assert the caller it returns is the dev person.

No test for R6, R9, R10 and R17 — they are document content or a dependency listing, and nothing outside a test could change their outcome. R8 is a one-time setup act, and what protects it is the forwarder's allowlist, already covered.

features.title: Isolation layer
features.description: Shipped in hive-health PR #26 as src/hive_health/devcopy/. R1 through R6, R18 and R19.
features.requirements: Own data and credentials directories, no scheduler, localhost, every live-pointing secret repointed, push subscriptions removed and notification permission declined, the auth-failure state recorded as a dev-only condition, a complete WAL-inclusive database copy minus the two sanitised items, and a local stand-in verifier.
features.acceptance_criteria: The live trees are out of reach by construction, not by convention.
features.qa_tests: The guard tests are the load-bearing ones: a symlink inside the dev root pointing at the live database is refused, judged on the resolved path, and the test deliberately avoids the live literal so the guard cannot be a string comparison asserted against itself.

stories.title: Build the dev-copy isolation layer
stories.description: Own data and credentials directories, no scheduler, localhost, secrets repointed, push removed, a WAL-inclusive copy, and a stand-in verifier. Verified 2026-10-01 against 21,963 measurements and 3,712 scores with a 6.6 MB WAL, three push subscriptions becoming none, an empty 0700 credentials directory, and the live database's mtime unmoved.
stories.acceptance_criteria: All eight met and verified on the running copy.
stories.qa_tests: Covered by PR #26's suite: copy completeness across every table in db.SCHEMA, AuthFailure from the real read_token, nothing sent from the real push.send, dev paths resolving inside the dev root, the exact non-scheduler task set, the dev settings' eight values, the guard refusing a foreign target and admitting a dev one, and the dev verifier resolving to the dev person.

features.title: The comms forwarder
features.description: R7 and R8. The dev copy reaches the real hive-comms through a local forwarder with a single-conversation allowlist.
features.requirements: Pass only calls aimed at the one nominated walkthrough conversation; refuse a reply or rename aimed at another, and any request to open a new one. The nominated conversation is created once by hand against the haiku provider, pinned into the dev database, and never held by Telegram or any other surface.
features.acceptance_criteria: The forwarder is what protects the one-time setup act, which is why R8 needs no test of its own.
features.qa_tests: Four tests: a foreign reply refused with nothing reaching the transport, a foreign rename refused, a request with no conversation id refused, and the nominated id passed through with its body intact. Verified live: 403 on a foreign conversation and on a new-conversation request, and the nominated one reaching the real gateway.

stories.title: Build the single-conversation forwarder
stories.description: Refuses a foreign reply, a foreign rename and any new conversation; passes the nominated one through.
stories.acceptance_criteria: 403 on everything but the nominated conversation.
stories.qa_tests: Four tests, plus live verification against the real gateway.

stories.title: Create and pin the nominated haiku conversation
stories.description: Outstanding. Requirement 8 is enforced — the forwarder's allowlist is in place — but the conversation itself is not yet created. It is created once by hand against the haiku provider, pinned into the dev database, and never held by Telegram or any other surface.
stories.requirements: Created against haiku, pinned, never adopted by another surface.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The walkthrough has a real conversation to adopt, rename and recolour.
stories.qa_tests: The walkthrough's adopt, rename and recolour steps reach the real gateway and succeed. A conversation held by Telegram would break the exclusivity R8 requires, so confirm no surface owns it.

features.title: The manifest and the report
features.description: Shipped in PR #27 as tools/walkthrough/ and docs/behaviour-manifest.md. R10 through R17.
features.requirements: The unit is a view rather than a screen, so sub-tabs, period selectors and data states can each be numbered. Unique stable numbers, with the parser refusing duplicates. A bug marker that excludes a behaviour from the oracle. An uncovered marker the coverage checker honours. Unreachable routes named rather than silently absent. Per-behaviour pass, fail or uncovered reporting. One step list for both run modes. Playwright in requirements-dev.txt.
features.acceptance_criteria: The manifest holds sixteen views and fifty-two behaviours — nine bugs, six uncovered — and names all twenty API routes no view reaches.
features.qa_tests: R12's test is the one that keeps the oracle honest: the oracle's behaviour set equals exactly the non-bug behaviours of a manifest holding one of each, so a bug frozen as a requirement would fail it. R13's distinguishes an honest uncovered marker from a gap.
